passages.title: Academic Knowledge vs. Employability Skills
passages.subtitle: How vocational colleges and universities prepare young people for the labour market
paragraphs: For many generations, universities focused mostly on academic study. Courses were largely theoretical, meaning students spent their years reading classic books, attending lectures, and writing research papers. However, today's labour market moves fast, and many business owners complain that young graduates are not job-ready when they arrive at their first office.

When companies interview young applicants, they look closely for two sets of skills. First, they want practical skills, such as building websites, checking budgets, or using modern design tools. Second, they value soft skills like clear speaking, working calmly in teams, and managing time well. Many managers say a candidate with good soft skills can quickly learn company rules, even without top university grades.

Because of this demand, vocational schools are growing in popularity. Unlike traditional universities, vocational programmes train students directly for real jobs such as bakery chef, solar panel installer, dental assistant, or IT technician. Learners spend most of their week practising in training kitchens, clinics, or garages, and many receive job offers before they even finish their final term.

Still, defenders of university education warn that schools should not drop academic subjects. Studying history, science, or economics teaches people how to ask smart questions, check reliable facts, and solve unfamiliar problems. While a specific software tool might be replaced in three years, clear thinking stays useful across many different careers.

Today, many countries are trying to blend the best parts of both paths. In Austria and Switzerland, dual-training programmes let students spend part of the week in college classes and the rest of the week working at a local business for a monthly wage. Meanwhile, more universities are adding short workplace projects and career coaching so students graduate with both deep knowledge and real experience.

passages.title: Why Fewer Students Choose Science
passages.subtitle: Exploring the STEM shortage, career choices, and ways to inspire young scientists
paragraphs: A Modern life depends heavily on technological advancement, from clean wind power to life-saving hospital equipment. Yet in many countries, universities are worried because fewer teenagers are applying for STEM courses—science, technology, engineering, and mathematics. Business groups warn that this shortage of skilled graduates could slow down new inventions and make it hard to repair essential power and water systems.

B Why are students turning away from science? One common reason is that subjects like physics and chemistry are perceived as difficult. Many secondary schools do not have modern laboratory gear, so teenagers spend most lessons copying long notes and memorising complex rules. Students who want high final grades for university often drop science and pick subjects they feel more confident passing.

C Another reason is the promise of faster money in other industries. Many students picture scientific work as quiet, slow, and poorly paid. As a result, young people who are strong at mathematics often choose lucrative careers in banking, digital marketing, or law instead, believing these jobs offer quicker promotions and higher starting pay.

D Gender choices also make the STEM gap bigger. Although teenage girls often get top scores in school science and maths exams, far fewer women choose university degrees in robotics, software coding, or civil engineering. Researchers note two key reasons for this: old social habits still suggest that technical machines are mainly for boys, and school textbooks rarely include stories about famous female inventors.

E Luckily, schools can change how students feel about science. When teachers replace boring note-copying with fun science fairs, coding clubs, and team challenges—like building a small solar boat or testing local rainwater—students become much more curious. Seeing how science helps protect animals or keep people healthy makes lessons feel meaningful.

F Governments and tech firms are also helping outside the classroom. Some regions pay extra bonuses to recruit qualified physics teachers for small towns, while engineering groups run free weekend camps where teenage girls meet friendly women engineers. With better teaching and fairer pay, more students may choose to build the technology of the future.

passages.title: Parental Pressure and Children's Mental Health
passages.subtitle: Why scheduled activities should not replace unstructured free play
paragraphs: In many cities today, a ten-year-old's weekly diary looks busier than an office manager's. Right after school finishes, children rush from maths coaching to violin practice, chess club, and swimming lessons. Loving parents arrange these tight schedules because they worry about future jobs and want to give their children every possible advantage.

Setting high expectations can actually help children succeed. Education studies show that when parents take an interest in homework and cheer their children on, students try harder and feel proud of their progress. The problem begins when encouragement turns into heavy academic pressure. If parents scold children for every B grade or compare them constantly with top classmates, learning stops feeling joyful and starts feeling frightening.

Child counsellors warn that constant stress damages mental health. Increasingly, young teenagers visit clinics with headaches, poor sleep, and burnout—feeling completely tired and empty from nonstop work. Heavy criticism can also hurt a child's self-esteem. Instead of becoming brave learners, worried kids become scared of looking foolish, so they stop asking questions or trying hard tasks.

At the same time, busy after-school schedules have pushed out free play. Decades ago, kids rode bikes with friends, built treehouses, and made up street games without adults watching every move. Today, many parents worry that unscheduled afternoons are a waste of time and prefer organised classes that hand out medals and certificates.

Dr. Anna Novak, a family counsellor in Prague, believes losing free play is a big mistake. 'Unstructured play is how children grow into well-rounded people,' she says. 'When kids invent games without a coach, they learn to share, solve small fights, and bounce back when they lose.' Free time also gives tired young minds a chance to rest and discover personal hobbies.

Of course, parents should still guide their children and care about schoolwork. However, families need a healthier balance. Celebrating steady effort, keeping at least one afternoon a week completely free, and letting children choose their own hobbies can protect young minds. A calm, happy child is much more ready for future success than a stressed perfectionist.
